segments.text: explain pooled CRISPR screens to me

Pooled CRISPR screens are one of the most powerful tools in functional genomics. Here's a rigorous breakdown:

The Core Idea

You introduce a library of thousands of different guide RNAs into a large population of cells — all at once, in a single experiment — such that each cell receives (ideally) exactly one guide RNA. You then apply a selection pressure, and ask: which guides got enriched or depleted?

The readout is sequencing the guide RNA distribution before vs. after selection.

The Setup

1. Library design
You synthesize an oligo library encoding thousands of sgRNAs targeting, say, every gene in the genome (~3–10 guides per gene for redundancy). This library is cloned into a lentiviral vector that also encodes Cas9 or is delivered into cells already expressing Cas9.

2. Transduction at low MOI
Cells are infected at a multiplicity of infection ~0.3, meaning most infected cells get just one viral integration. This is critical — if a cell gets two guides, you can't attribute its phenotype to either one.

3. Maintain library representation
You need enough cells at every step so that each guide is represented by enough cells to give statistical power. A common rule of thumb is 500–1000 cells per guide. For a 100,000-guide library, that's 50–100 million cells minimum. This is a real practical constraint.

4. Apply selection
This is where screens diverge:

Survival/proliferation screens — the simplest. Cells that drop out of the population when a gene is knocked out reveal essential genes. You just passage cells over time.

Drug resistance screens — add a drug, see which KOs confer resistance or sensitization.

Reporter screens — a fluorescent reporter tied to a pathway; sort cells by GFP high vs. low via FACS.

FACS-based screens on any surface marker — sort on CD whatever, protein expression, etc.

5. Readout: deep sequencing
Extract genomic DNA, PCR-amplify the guide RNA cassette, and sequence. Count how many reads you get per guide. Compare the distribution before and after selection.

The Statistics

You're not looking at individual guides in isolation. You're aggregating signal across multiple guides targeting the same gene. If 6/6 guides against Gene X all deplete in a survival screen, that's a strong signal. If only 1/6 does, that's probably noise or an off-target effect.

Common analysis tools: MAGeCK is the standard. It uses a negative binomial model to call significant hits, accounting for guide-level variance. Output is a gene-level p-value and log fold change.

Arrayed vs. Pooled — the key tradeoff

In an arrayed screen, each well gets one guide. You can read out complex phenotypes per well (imaging, metabolomics, etc.) but it's enormously expensive and low throughput.

In a pooled screen, everything is mixed. You gain massive scale and cost efficiency, but your readout must be reducible to cell sorting or survival — you can't read out complex per-cell phenotypes directly. (This is why paired approaches like Perturb-seq exist — pooled genetic perturbation + single-cell RNA sequencing to get transcriptomic readouts per perturbation.)

Common failure modes worth knowing

Poor library representation — if you lose coverage during the screen, your statistics collapse

High MOI — cells with multiple guides give uninterpretable results

Insufficient guide diversity per gene — essential for distinguishing on-target signal from off-target toxicity

Selection too strong or too fast — can cause non-specific dropout

Cell type matters enormously — Cas9 editing efficiency and guide activity vary hugely across cell types; this is a real issue in hard-to-transfect cells like neurons or iPSCs

What's your angle on this — are you thinking about designing one, interpreting screen data, or understanding it conceptually for a different purpose? That changes what's worth going deeper on.

how do you synthesis such a massive set og sgrnas?

Good question — this is one of those details that's easy to gloss over but matters a lot practically.

Array Synthesis (the dominant method)

The standard approach is DNA microarray-based oligonucleotide synthesis. Companies like Twist Bioscience, Agilent, and CustomArray synthesize thousands to hundreds of thousands of distinct oligos in parallel on a chip, then cleave and pool them.

Each oligo encodes one sgRNA spacer sequence (~20nt), flanked by constant adapter sequences used for cloning. The full oligo is typically 60–80nt total.

The key limitation is synthesis error rate — each position has ~0.5–1% error probability, so a 70nt oligo might have only ~50% perfect sequences. This is why:

Libraries are sequenced after cloning to verify representation

You can't use this for applications requiring perfect single-stranded fidelity without additional QC

From Oligo Pool → Lentiviral Library

The pooled oligos go through several steps:

PCR amplification of the pool using the constant flanking adapters as primer binding sites — this gives you enough mass to work with

Cloning into a lentiviral backbone (typically via Gibson Assembly or restriction-ligation) upstream of the scaffold sequence. The scaffold is already in the vector; you're just inserting the spacer.

Bacterial transformation — here's a critical constraint: you need to transform enough colonies to maintain library representation. If your library has 100,000 guides, you need >1 million colonies to ensure ~10x coverage at the bacterial stage, or you'll have dropout before you even touch a mammalian cell.

Plasmid maxiprep → lentiviral packaging → titer → transduce cells

Why Representation Can Collapse Early

The PCR amplification step in (1) can introduce non-uniform amplification — some sequences amplify better than others due to secondary structure or GC content. This is a known source of skew in final libraries, and why library QC sequencing before the screen is non-optional, not optional.

The Scaffold Isn't Synthesized Each Time

Worth being explicit: you're not synthesizing the full sgRNA sequence in the oligo pool. You're synthesizing only the variable 20nt spacer (plus adapters). The invariant scaffold sequence lives in the vector. This keeps oligo length tractable.

One thing worth sitting with: the whole system is remarkably fragile at each handoff — synthesis errors, PCR bias, transformation efficiency, lentiviral titer uniformity, MOI control. A screen that works is the product of many things going right simultaneously, which is part of why replication and good controls matter so much in interpreting screen hits.

further explain this. I don't understand how, at the end of the screen, you determine which guides edited which cells

This is a really important conceptual point, and the answer is that you don't determine which guides edited which cells individually. The logic is population-level, not single-cell.

Let me break down exactly what's happening:

What's Actually in the Cells

When you transduce your library lentivirally, the guide RNA cassette integrates into the genome of each cell. This is key — the sgRNA sequence becomes a permanent, heritable barcode in that cell and all its descendants.

So when you lyse your cells at the end of the screen and extract genomic DNA, every cell has contributed its guide sequence to that DNA pool.

The PCR Step

You design primers that flank the integrated guide cassette — binding to the constant vector sequences on either side of the variable 20nt spacer. These primers amplify the spacer region from every cell in your population simultaneously.

What you get is a PCR product pool where the relative abundance of each amplicon reflects the relative abundance of that guide in your cell population.

The Sequencing + Counting Logic

You sequence this pool deeply (tens of millions of reads), then count how many reads correspond to each guide sequence. This gives you a frequency distribution across all guides.

You compare two timepoints:

T0: right after transduction (or early passaging), before selection

T-end: after your selection pressure

If guide X against Gene Y went from 0.01% of reads → 0.001% of reads, cells carrying that guide dropped out — meaning knocking out Gene Y was deleterious under your conditions.

If it went from 0.01% → 0.1%, those cells were enriched — the knockout provided a competitive advantage.

The Core Assumption

The entire logic rests on one assumption: the integrated guide sequence is a faithful proxy for what perturbation that cell experienced. You're inferring the genotype from the barcode, not measuring the edit directly.

This is why low MOI is so critical — if a cell has two integrated guides, its guide sequence is ambiguous and its phenotype is uninterpretable.

What You Never Know

Whether Cas9 actually cut efficiently in any given cell

Whether the edit was a frameshift vs. in-frame indel (functional KO vs. not)

The exact edit each cell carries

This is a real limitation. Incomplete editing means your KO population is actually a mix of true KOs and partial/no-edit cells, which dilutes your signal. This is partly why you need multiple guides per gene — consistent signal across all of them provides evidence that the effect is real and not driven by editing variability.

The whole thing is essentially a competitive fitness assay with molecular barcodes. Does that framing clarify the logic?

Pros of Keeping a Senior Recruiter in Charge of HR Assistance:
1. Expertise in the recruitment process: A senior recruiter is well-versed in talent acquisition strategies and can contribute valuable insights to the HR assistance process.
2. Familiarity with company culture: A senior recruiter understands the intricacies of the company culture and can align the administrative support accordingly.
3. Strong relationship with hiring managers: A senior recruiter has established relationships with hiring managers, enabling efficient collaboration and understanding of their needs.
4. Proven track record: A senior recruiter has a successful history of sourcing and acquiring top talent, ensuring the best candidates are selected for open positions.

Cons of Keeping a Senior Recruiter in Charge of HR Assistance:
1. Time constraints: As administrative duties increase, the senior recruiter may face time constraints, impacting their ability to focus on recruitment activities.
2. Competing priorities: Balancing administrative tasks and recruitment goals may lead to a dilution of efforts and potential compromises in both areas.
3. Limited expertise in administrative functions: While a senior recruiter may have general knowledge of administrative tasks, their expertise may not match that of a dedicated administrative professional.
4. Misalignment with strategic HR needs: The growing administrative workload may lead to a misalignment with the strategic HR goals of the company, potentially impacting long-term recruitment success.

Write an hour long story of a man describing in detail their transformation into a car.

Once there lived a man named Max. He was a simple man, with an uneventful life. Max worked a desk job, had a mundane social life, and lived alone in a small apartment. However, one day, everything changed. Max woke up one morning feeling a strange sensation throughout his body. He felt his skin prickling, and his limbs rustling.

Alarmed, Max got up from his bed and noticed he was much taller than usual. He watched, transfixed, as his hands morphed into wheel-like versions, and his feet fused together and formed a smooth base. His arms expanded into the body of the car, and his fingers elongated, becoming wheels. Within minutes, Max had turned into a car.

At first, Max was terrified, but as he began to move around, he started to feel more comfortable. He zipped around his apartment, testing his new car features. The wheels on Max's feet allowed him to move at lightning speed, and the lights on his forehead became functional headlights. The rear ended shaped into an exhaust, and the roof lifted to reveal a rack for carrying luggage.

Max motivated by his surreal transformation, decided to venture out into the world as a car. He zoomed through the streets, feeling the cool air rush through the car's "windows". As he drove onwards, he saw creatures on the road; some laughed and others gawked at the strange sight. But Max was undeterred. He was having too much fun.

The sensation of steering the car with his feet and hands was thrilling. Within hours, Max had driven hundreds of miles, completely fearless of the journey. He laughed excitedly, watching the world go by, enjoying the freedom that his newfound car body afforded him.

Days became weeks, and Max quickly realized that he never wanted to go back to his old life, even if he could. Max had made a new life as a car. He could travel anywhere he wanted, never had to worry about traffic, paid no insurance cost, and knew no rules. He had unlimited power and could indulge himself in new adventures anytime.

Max's story traveled across the globe, inspiring others who were stuck in the routine of life. And, before anyone knew it, a new breed of people had emerged, the car people, as they preferred to be called.

Car Max lived an exciting life, full of adventure, and never missed his old life ever again. He became the legend, the first car man, and the pioneer of new extraordinary transformations.

The car seemed to have a mind of its own. It drove erratically, swerving and jerking on the roads. The car carried Max faster than he had ever gone before. He screamed with fear as he watched the world go by, with the car rolling on its own.

As the days went by, Max realized that he was no longer in control at all. The car seemed to be possessed, and no matter how hard Max tried, he could not escape the machine's clutches. The car now had him, and he was trapped inside with no way out.

The sensation of steering the car with his feet and hands was no longer thrilling. It had become a nightmare, with Max feeling trapped, unable to escape the confines of his new body. Within hours, Max had driven hundreds of miles, completely powerless of the journey. He saw a strange darkness inside the car, as if it was a different world, a world from which Max couldn't escape.

Days became weeks, and Max quickly realized that he never wanted to be this car, even if he could. Max had made a new life as a car, unknowingly cursed, unable to control his fate. He could travel anywhere he wanted, never had to worry about traffic, paid no insurance cost, and knew no rules. But, he was trapped in this new reality; car Max was forever a prisoner in his own mind.

Max's story traveled across the globe, frightening others who were stuck in the routine of life. And, before anyone knew it, a new breed of curse had emerged, the car people, as they preferred to call it.

Max now lived an endless nightmare, full of terror and pain, and never missed his old life ever again. He became the legend, the cursed car man, and the pioneer of dark and horrifying transformations.

What was the Great Sanhedrin of 1808?

The Great Sanhedrin of 1808 was a Jewish assembly convened by Napoleon Bonaparte, who was then the Emperor of the French. It was a gathering of Jewish leaders from across Europe, mainly from the territories that were under French control at that time. The purpose of the Great Sanhedrin was to determine the legal status of Jews and to address various questions regarding their religious practices and integration into French society.

The Sanhedrin had not been convened since the time of ancient Judea, and Napoleon saw its revival as a way to establish a centralized body that could represent and organize Jewish communities. The assembly consisted of 71 rabbis and laymen. They were tasked with answering a series of questions regarding Jewish law, customs, and practices, as well as issues of Jewish loyalty and patriotism to the French state.

The Great Sanhedrin produced a report known as the "Answers of the Sanhedrin." This report affirmed the loyalty of French Jews to the French state and emphasized their desire to integrate into French society. It also asserted that Judaism did not conflict with the principles of the French Revolution and advocated for the full equality of Jews before the law.

The Great Sanhedrin of 1808 had a significant impact on the legal status of Jews in France and other parts of Europe. Napoleon subsequently issued the Decree of March 17, 1808, which granted Jews citizenship and equal rights under the law in French territories. This was a significant step towards Jewish emancipation and helped to pave the way for the recognition of Jewish rights in other European countries.
Why was hewed stone so important in ancient Israel, Judah, and Judea?

Hewed stone was important in ancient Israel, Judah, and Judea for several reasons:

1. Symbolic and religious significance: In ancient Israelite society, hewed stone was often associated with religious structures. Stone was considered a durable and timeless material, which made it fitting for constructing sacred spaces, such as temples, altars, and the Ark of the Covenant. The use of hewed stone emphasized the importance and permanence of these structures in the worship and religious life of the ancient Israelites.

2. Architectural strength and longevity: Hewed stone provided strength and durability to buildings. Large stones were carefully shaped and fitted together, creating stable and long-lasting structures. This was crucial in a time when construction techniques were limited and materials were scarce. The use of hewed stone allowed for the creation of solid and enduring buildings that could withstand the test of time.

3. Economic and political significance: The availability of quality stone for construction was a reflection of a region's wealth and power. Ancient Israel, Judah, and Judea were known for their limestone and other types of stone that were suitable for hewing. The ability to quarry and shape stone allowed these regions to build impressive cities, fortresses, and defensive walls. These monumental structures not only demonstrated the strength and prosperity of the Israelite kingdoms but also served as symbols of their political and military might.

4. Artistic and aesthetic appeal: Hewed stone allowed for the creation of intricate architectural details and decorative elements. Skilled craftsmen could carve intricate designs, inscriptions, and reliefs onto the surface of hewed stones, adding beauty and artistic value to buildings. These embellishments served both decorative and communicative purposes, showcasing the cultural and artistic achievements of ancient Israelite society.

In summary, hewed stone held immense significance in ancient Israel, Judah, and Judea due to its symbolic, religious, architectural, economic, and artistic importance. ]


Now, we create the main game loop:

```python
while True:
    next_key = w.getch()
    key = key if next_key == -1 else next_key

    if snake[0] == food:
        food = None
        while food is None:
            nf = [
                random.randint(1, sh - 1),

            ]
            food = nf if nf not in snake else None
        w.addch(food[0], food[1], curses.ACS_PI)

        w.addch(int(tail[0]), int(tail[1]), ' ')
```
